name: Dusky Auricula Purple
lede: Dusky Auricula Purple is a dark, grayed purple first plated by Robert Ridgway in 1912, its name likely built on the auricula, a primrose grown for purple-shaded petals.

sections.title: A flower's name, darkened
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* of 1912 plates this swatch at plate XXVI, hue 69 prime, on an aged, scanned original that is itself approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS charts of 1955 file block 242 as a dark reddish purple, 4.2 units from this swatch [1]. The name pairs *dusky* with [[auricula-purple|Auricula Purple]]; the base name's own origin is undocumented in our sources, but it likely points to *Primula auricula*, a European primrose grown for petals that shade from purple toward near-black at the throat [1].

At hex #5E4556 it measures lightness 33 and chroma 15 in LCH [1]. Its closest named neighbor is [[eggplant|Eggplant]], 2.9 units away and redder; [[dark-maroon-purple|Dark Maroon Purple]] sits 4.3 units off, also redder, and [[dusty-plum|Dusty Plum]] 5.0 units off, lighter and redder [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 0.28% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (67 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 38 [3]. In our archive it is rarer than 54% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.7% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (12 paintings), 3.0 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 50% of its 38 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. The earliest match dates to 1375, 537 years before the name's 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
